about: Your screen can't feel your finger. Test film in the cutaway-explainer format studied from @scroll.engineer's Apple Watch reel (Nov 9 2026; see LESSONS.md). Tech, explained, How tech works. One hard idea: a phone's touchscreen senses the charge your conductive finger pulls from a grid of see-through electrodes, not pressure. So a wool glove does nothing, and water can fake a tap. Sources: Densitron, 'Projected capacitive touch sensor' (densitron.com/news/projected-capacitive-touch-sensor): a finger near the sensor changes the local field and reduces the mutual capacitance; Renesas white paper 'Capacitive touch solutions for wearable applications' (renesas.com/tw/en/document/whp/white-papercapacitive-touch-solutions-wearable-applications): for mutual-capacitance pads a finger causes a decrease in capacitance. Scope: the hook is about the touch layer; iPhone 3D Touch (6s–XS, 2015–2018) had a separate pressure sensor, dropped since. Facts: projected capacitive touch (mutual capacitance): transparent indium tin oxide row and column electrodes under the cover glass; the touch controller scans every crossing; a nearby conductive finger reduces the mutual capacitance at the crossings under it, and the controller interpolates the centroid as the touch point. Phones report touch at 120 Hz or more (iPhone 120 Hz touch sampling, many Android phones 240 Hz+), so 'over a hundred times a second' is a floor. Water is conductive and is the known cause of ghost touches on wet screens. Narration-led: lines laid out by voiceover.py layout, every beat keyed to word times.

lines.text: Your screen can't feel you pressing it.
lines.say: Your screen, can't feel you pressing it.

lines.text: It feels your finger pull on its electric field.
lines.say: It feels your finger, pull on its electric field.

lines.text: That's why, with gloves on, you tap and nothing happens.
So what is the screen actually sensing?
Under the glass sits a grid of see-through wires.
Every crossing holds a tiny electric field. The phone checks them over a hundred times a second.
lines.say: Every crossing holds a tiny electric field, the phone checks them over a hundred times a second.

lines.text: Your finger is mostly salty water, so it conducts.
Bring it close, and it pulls away some of that field.
The phone finds which crossings dropped, and their center is your tap.
A wool glove doesn't conduct, so nothing drops.
But there's a catch. Water conducts too.
lines.say: But there's a catch, water conducts too.

lines.text: That's why rain can tap things for you.
So your screen isn't feeling a push. It's feeling you.
lines.say: So your screen isn't feeling a push, it's feeling you.

lines.text: Has your screen ever gone crazy in the rain?
lines.say: Has your screen, ever gone crazy in the rain?
